title: A version of Helly's theorem without convexity but connectivity
text:
It's more than 100 years since Helly's celebrated theorem in discrete geometry was published by him, and yet ghosts still remain. The theorem in it's infinitary glory states

Let $\{X_j\}_{j\in J}$ be a collection of compact, convex sets in $R^d$ such that every subcollection of size at most $d+1$ have non-empty intersection, then the whole collection has non-empty intersection.

One can show that the compactness condition is necessary in some form. For example in $\mathbb R$, one can look at the family of intervals $I_n=[n,\infty)$. These are convex and any two of them have an intersection (they are nested), but the whole family has empty intersection. Although it is known that compactness can be weakened to all sets are closed and at least one of them is bounded.
People have generalised this to massive extents. One of them is via something called the $(p,q)$ property with respect to some set.

Definition : A family of sets $\mathcal F$ is said to satisfy the $(p,q)$ condition with resepct to a set $\mathcal T$ (called the transversal set) if for any $p\ge q$ sets from $\mathcal F$ (say $\mathcal F_p$), there exists $q$ sets in $\mathcal F_p$ that can be hit by a single set in $\mathcal T$ (hit by a set means has non-empty intersection with)

In this language, Helly's theorem reduces to saying that if a family of compact, convex sets in $\mathbb R^d$ has the $(d+1, d+1)$ property with respect to points, then the family can be hit by a single point.
What is interesting is looking at the transversal set to be hyperplanes. Alon and Kalai has shown the following.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a countable family of compact, convex sets in $\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $(p,q)$ property with respect to the set of all hyperplanes ($p\ge q\ge d+1$). Then there exists a constant $c$ (depending only on $p, q$ and $d$) such that $\mathcal F$ can be hit by at most $c$ many hyperplanes.

As a challenge, I wanted to see how far can the conditions be dropped. Compactness cannot be dropped (it has to be there in some form) as the family of open balls $B_n$ in $\mathbb R^2$ with center at $(n,1/n)$ and radius $1/n$ have the $(3,3)$ property with respect to lines, but cannot be hit by finitely many lines.
So I wanted to drop convexity and try adding just connectivity (and also work in $d\ge 2$ just so that the example is not too trivial). My gut feeling tells me the statement won't hold, but this is turning out to be very very hard for some reason.
So the question I really want to ask is whether there is a counterexample for this

Let $\mathcal F$ be a countable family of compact, connected sets in $\mathbb R^d$ ($d\ge 2$) satisfying $(p,d+1)$ property with respect to the set of all hyperplanes ($p\ge d+1$). Then there exists a constant $c$ (depending only on $p$ and $d$) such that $\mathcal F$ can be hit by at most $c$ many hyperplanes.

title: Double derivative representation in terms of $\theta$?
text:
Ok, this is a thought I had, as we all know that we can write $\mathrm dy/\mathrm dx$ as $\tan(\theta)$ because it's just the slope of the tangent line. Thought I could get the double derivative in terms of $\theta$ as well, so I took the equation $\mathrm dy/\mathrm dx = \tan(\theta)$ and differentiated both sides with respect to $x$, so I got $\mathrm d^2y/\mathrm dx^2 = [\sec(\theta)]^2\mathrm d\theta/\mathrm dx$. For $\mathrm d\theta/\mathrm dx$, I referred to the original equation $\tan\theta = \mathrm dy/\mathrm dx$; this implies that $θ = \arctan(\mathrm dy/\mathrm dx)$. Subbing this in at $\mathrm d\theta$, I get this:
$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\tan\theta
\\
\\\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\sec^2\theta \frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dx}
\\
\theta = \arctan\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)
\\
\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\sec^2\theta \frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dx}
\\
\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\sec^2\theta~ \frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)^2}~\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
\\
1=1
$$
The problem is that through the chain rule, there is a $\mathrm d^2y/\mathrm dx^2$ at the end of the last equation, and since $\mathrm dy/\mathrm dx$ is $\tan\theta$ subbing, that cancels everything out and gives $1=1$. I want to know if I am wrong or if I am abusing the differentials as fractions too much. Also, please tell me if there is a better way of approaching the problem of double derivative in terms of $\theta$.

title: Does this correctly show that there is an affine transformation that takes a circle in the plane (arbitrarily close) to a parabola?
text:
I believe this is essentially just a way to show that there is an anisotropic scaling of a circle that produces an ellipse arbitrarily close to a parabola.
Let $u \in [0,2\pi)$, $R \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$
Let $$\Phi:\mathbb{R^2}\times [0,\frac{\pi}{4}) \rightarrow \mathbb{R^2}$$ be given by $$\Phi(x,y,t)=\left(\frac{1+\tan(t+\frac{\pi}{4})}{2\sqrt{\tan(t+\frac{\pi}{4})}}x,\frac{1+\tan(t+\frac{\pi}{4})}{2}y\right)$$
If we choose some $t_1 \in [0,\frac{\pi}{4})$ then the map $\Phi(x,y,t_1)$ is just an anisotropic scaling of the $xy$-plane.
If we choose some $t_2 \in [0,\frac{\pi}{4})$ arbitrarily close to $\frac{\pi}{4}$, then $$\Phi(R\cos(u),R+R\sin(u),t_2)$$ comes arbitrarily close to parametrizing the parabola $y=\frac{x^2}{R}$, as can be seen in my simulation
Thus, the affine transformation $$\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1+\tan(t_2+\frac{\pi}{4})}{2\sqrt{\tan(t_2+\frac{\pi}{4})}} & 0 \\\ 0 & \frac{1+\tan(t_2+\frac{\pi}{4})}{2}\end{bmatrix}$$ comes arbitrarily close to taking the circle given by $x^2+(y-R)^2=R^2$ to the parabola $y=\frac{x^2}{R}$

title: How to prove injectivity? An infinite set $E$ is bijective to $\mathbb{N}$ (Royden "Real Analysis Third Edition")
text:
On p.21 in "Real Analysis Third Edition" by H. L. Royden.

if an infinite set $E$ is the range of a sequence $\langle x_n\rangle$, then $E$ can be put in one-to-one correspondence with $\mathbb{N}$. To do this we define a function $\varphi$ from $\mathbb{N}$ into $\mathbb{N}$ by recursion as follows: Let $\varphi(1)=1$, and define $\varphi(n+1)$ to be the smallest value of $m$ such that $x_m\neq x_i$ for all $i\leq \varphi(n)$. Since $E$ is infinite, such an $m$ always exists, and by the well-ordering principle for $\mathbb{N}$ there is always a least such $m$. The correspondence $n\mapsto x_{\varphi(n)}$ is a one-to-one correspondence between $\mathbb{N}$ and $E$.

I tried to prove this fact as follows.

By the definition of $\varphi$, $\varphi(n)<\varphi(n+1)$ for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
I want to prove the correspondence $n\mapsto x_{\varphi(n)}$ is injective.
The following is a proof of surjectivity.
Let $x_{i_1}\in E$.
Then, there is $n_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\varphi(n_1)\leq i_1<\varphi(n_1+1)$.
Since $i_1<\varphi(n_1+1)$, $x_{i_1}=x_{i_2}$ for some $i_2\leq\varphi(n_1)$.
If $\varphi(n_1)=i_2$, then $n_1\mapsto x_{\varphi(n_1)}=x_{i_2}=x_{i_1}$.
Suppose that $\varphi(n_1)>i_2$.
There is $n_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\varphi(n_2)\leq i_2<\varphi(n_2+1)$ and $n_2<n_1$.
Since $i_2<\varphi(n_2+1)$, $x_{i_2}=x_{i_3}$ for some $i_3\leq\varphi(n_2)$.
If $\varphi(n_2)=i_3$, then $n_2\mapsto x_{\varphi(n_2)}=x_{i_3}=x_{i_2}=x_{i_1}$.
Suppose that $\varphi(n_2)>i_3$.
There is $n_3\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\varphi(n_3)\leq i_3<\varphi(n_3+1)$ and $n_3<n_2$.
$\dots$
There is no sequence $\langle n_i\rangle$ such that $n_i\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n_1>n_2>n_3>\cdots$.
So, the correspondence $n\mapsto x_{\varphi(n)}$ is surjective.

How to prove injectivity?

Since $x_{\varphi(n+1)}\neq x_i$ for all $i\leq\varphi(n)$, $x_{\varphi(n+1)}\neq x_{\varphi(i)}$ for $i\leq n$ because $\varphi(i)\leq\varphi(n)$ if $i\leq n$.
So, the correspondence $n\mapsto x_{\varphi(n)}$ is injective.
Is this ok?

title: What even is the notion of a function growing faster than one another? What defines the fastness (or degree) of a function's growth?
text:
The Context:
I was reading the book The Road to Reality by Roger Penrose when in his calculus section he gave a paragraph or two about the notion of $C^{\infty}$-smoothness and there was one exercise that asked us to prove this infinitely derived continuity of a puzzling function:
$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix}
x>0:&e^{-1/x} \\ 
x\leq 0: & 0
\end{matrix}\right.$$
The question in the book was labeled as difficult and recommended for those with good experience with analysis. Presumably, this could have meant, Real Analysis students or well-off calculus students, which is what I thought I was.
I searched the web for a proof, and I found one that used the idea that for any nth derivative of this piecewise, for the function to be continuous there, the limit of the function towards $0^+$ with $0^-$ (or just $0$ from both sides)  must match. This makes intuitive sense and uses an argument of neighborhoods, which I have just accepted as an internal axiom at this point in my career.
The argument came down to show the fact that the derivative will always take the form of this composed exponential multiplied by some polynomial that is composed with the reciprocal function. Then it was stated that the numerator tends to zero faster than the denominator tends to infinity. Which is saying that e^x is faster than any polynomial.
The Question:
My question is, what is a rigorous notion of 'fastness' or growth rate? I've seen that you can observe the asymptotic behavior of a function or its derivative to gain an insight on the ordering (order) of two functions and their growths, but I never really had a sense of rigorous intuition to give a complete, non-circular proof of how functions grow faster than others using a definition of 'growth rate' that doesn't include just a list of functions that are known to 'grow' faster than others.
The issue with my definition of growth is that in my mind it can mean multiple things. It can mean instantaneous rate of change, average rate of change, how fast a rate of change grows (or changes), or even what a function approaches asymptotically. It all seems to be not abstracted enough. (Like is there a number who can quantify the notion of fastness of a function?)
For example, the question of which grows faster between $f(x)=Ax\sin(x)$ and $g(x)=Bx$ seems to have ambiguities. It would be awesome to gain a better insight into this and maybe a more liberating way of thinking than the box I seem to be within. This question is also open to the discussion of sequences and series.

title: Confusion about the criteria for a complete metric space to be a length space
text:
According to corollary 2.4.17 from the textbook "A Course In Metric Geometry" we have
A complete metric space $(X, d)$ is a length space iff,
given a positive $\varepsilon$ and two points $x, y \in X$, there exists a finite sequence
of points $x = x_1, x_2,..., x_k = y$ such that every two neighboring points in
this sequence are $\varepsilon$-close (i.e., $d(x_i, x_{i+1}) \leq \varepsilon$ for all $i = 1,..., k − 1)$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} d(x_i, x_{i+1}) < d(x, y) + \varepsilon$.
However, I do not believe this claim to be correct. For example, the points $-1$ and $1$ as a sub metric space of $\mathbb{R}$. If we give this the induced Length Structure, then $d_L(1,-1) = \infty$ (because there are no continuous paths between $1$ and $-1$). This is also clearly a complete metric space because every Cauchy Sequence converges. However, there is no finite set of points between $1$ and $-1$ that is $\varepsilon$-close for any $\varepsilon > 0$. Is this a contradiction to the corollary? Do they mean to say a Complete, bounded metric space?

title: Mathematically Ranking Football Players
text:
Here is a math problem I thought of.

Suppose there are 100 football players. Let's assume that there is some objective ranking (i.e. true ranking) of these players that exist (e.g. p1 is best, p2 is second best ... p100 is worst). There are no ties in the true ranking

On any given day, a random set of these players come to the gymnasium to play football. They are randomly assigned to teams (the teams are randomly and unevenly divided, e.g. 11 players show up,  team 1 gets 9 players and team 2 gets 2 players) .

These players play a game of football and the final score is recorded.

We  ONLY have access to the final score and which players played on which teams.


I wrote an R program to simulate how this might look like for 100 games (this simulation just splits a subset of the players into 2 teams and randomly assigns a score to both teams as a proof of concept ... in this simulation, the results of the game are random and are not influenced by the true rankings of the players, the rankings of their team mates and the rankings of their opponents):
num_games <- 100

players <- paste0("p", 1:100)

results <- data.frame(game_no = integer(), 
                      team_1 = character(), 
                      team_2 = character(), 
                      score_team_1 = integer(), 
                      score_team_2 = integer(), 
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)



for(game in 1:num_games) {
    n1 <- sample(1:10, 1)
    n2 <- sample(1:10, 1)
    
    team1 <- sample(players, n1)
    remaining_players <- setdiff(players, team1)
    team2 <- sample(remaining_players, n2)
    
    score_team_1 <- sample(0:20, 1)
    score_team_2 <- sample(0:20, 1)
    
   
    team1_str <- paste(team1, collapse = ", ")
    team2_str <- paste(team2, collapse = ", ")
    
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(game_no = game, 
                                         team_1 = team1_str, 
                                         team_2 = team2_str, 
                                         score_team_1 = score_team_1, 
                                         score_team_2 = score_team_2))
}

head(results)

The game results might look like this:

       1           p69, p75, p27, p95, p42, p99, p28                          p35, p34, p92, p90           11            6

       4 p46, p51, p60, p62, p55, p22, p24, p12, p44 p99, p21, p70, p89, p56, p49, p75, p40, p20           12            6
       5      p71, p16, p83, p56, p26, p45, p38, p10                     p44, p11, p42, p57, p32           16           20
       6                                    p64, p19           p20, p79, p34, p39, p66, p38, p73           16           14

I have the following question:

Suppose we have data from 1000 games between these players. We are interested in estimating the individual rankings of each player (i.e. how good is "player x" in isolation). However, we only have information about the performance of players on a given team when playing another set of players.

We assume that the observed performance of players depends on who is on their team and who they are playing against. However, we are not assuming that teams made of more stronger players always perform better (e.g. "too many cooks in the kitchen spoil the broth" - perhaps some players have better synergy with other players, e.g. a team with a strong player and a medium player might win more against a team of 2 strong players)

For example, suppose p1 is best, p2 is second best ... p100 is worst. Let's say we have a matchup between team 1 (p8, p98, p99) vs team 2 (p2, p100). The final score could be 1-8 (team 1 - team 2). Here it would appear that player 100 is a strong player but this is only because he is playing with player 2. On the other hand, it might appear that player8 is a bad player, but this is only because he is playing with 2 really bad players against one of the best players.


Is there any mathematical algorithm (e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TrueSkill) that search through the available data and try to use some elimination/estimation procedure to try and estimate the individual rankings of players based on this set up?
I am wondering if something might exist which adjusts the ranking based on the availability of data we have on each player. For example, suppose player41 usually plays alone or at most with one other player. Presumably, we would be able to get a better idea of player41's ability compared to some other player that generally plays on bigger teams.

title: The shape of parabola in a 1-point perspective drawing with the vanishing point at the parabola's point at infinity
text:
Edit: After a little bit of careful construction, I've worked out that the map I should have been using instead is $$\phi\left(x,y\right)=\left(\frac{x}{ay+1},\frac{ay}{ay+1}\right)$$
where $a\in(0,\infty)$ determines the spacing between horizontal lines as well as the eccentricity of the ellipse. Choosing an $a$ value also determines to the "height" of the observer/camera/eye, and smoothly varying $a$ corresponds to moving the "camera" closer to or father away from the plane.
This would be the appropriate map for modeling 1-point perspective.
More generally, if we desire $(p,q)$ to be the coordinates of our vanishing point, then
$$\Phi(x,y)=\left(p+\frac{x}{ay+1},q-1+\frac{ay}{ay+1}\right)$$ for any $a>0$
See Constructing a map that accurately mimics 1-point perspective for a derivation of this result.

It is common to see introductory explanations of projective geometry that claim the following:

if you take a parabola in the plane and create a 1-point perspective drawing of it such that the vanishing point is at the parabola's point at infinity, then the parabola will appear as an ellipse in the perspective drawing $\tag1$


However, if you continue plotting the points $(n,n^2)$ for integers $n$ as I've started to in this picture, you will get a teardrop-like shape given by $x^2=(1-y)^2\log_{b}\left(1-y\right)$ for some $b\in(0,1)$, and not an ellipse.

As can be weakly verified by looking at my desmos simulation, the map $\Phi:\mathbb{R^3} \rightarrow \mathbb{R^2}$ given by $$\Phi(x,y,t)=(xt^y,1-t^y)$$
takes the point at infinity in the direction of the positive $y$-axis to $(0,1)$, and for $t\in(0,1)$ the map continuously deforms the $xy$-plane in such a way that exactly mimics looking down onto the $xy$-plane from a vantage point that continuously increases in height above the $xy$-plane as $t$ increases.
However, there is no $t \in (0,1)$ such that the curve parametrized in $x$ by $\Phi(x,x^2,t)=(xt^{x^2},1-t^{x^2})$ is an ellipse.
Does this prove that (1) is false and should be replaced with the following statement?

If you take a parabola and create a 1-point perspective drawing of it such that the vanishing point is at the parabola's point at infinity, then the parabola will appear as a teardrop-shaped curve in the perspective drawing $\tag2$


If instead of $(0,1)$ we desire $(p,q)$ to be the image of the point at infinity in the direction of the positive $y$-axis, then the map $\Phi$ can be modified to $\Phi(x,y,t)=(p+xt^y,q-t^y)$

title: Probability of Shuffling a Deck of Cards a Single Time from New Deck Order
text:
I have the following question about shuffling a deck of $52$ playing cards. Most people are astounded by the fact that $52!$ is a really big number, and they say that because it is so big that whenever a deck of cards is shuffled with high probability it is the first time that deck has been in that order.
My question has to do with what happens after the first shuffle. Let's say we start off with a brand new deck of playing cards, so it will be in new card order. If we apply a single riffle shuffle, then how many ways can this be done? But on a more practical note, is it probable that every such shuffle has occurred?
For simplicity, let us label the cards $1,2,3,...,52$. What I mean by a riffle shuffle is that we cut the deck into two piles say $1,...,x$ and $x+1,...,52$. Then we interweave the two decks together to form a sequence that has $1,2,...,x$ and $x+1,x+2,...,52$ as subsequences. At first, I thought that I would just look at all $52$ original cuts, and then count the number of such riffles for each one, but then I realized that I was overcounting as I could always return the cards into new card order for any such shuffle. Thus, I think it requires a bit more attention.
I believe we can just count the number of sequences as described above, but I don't know if there is a clever way of counting them (as I think the order matters since if the first card we put down is $x+1$ rather than $1$ these two scenarios seem to have different yet similar comparisons), and it might seem partitioning this space might be quite difficult. If someone has a clever way of counting this I'd be interested. Furthermore, is such a number going to be big enough that even after a single shuffle we should expect a "new" card order?
author: Steven Creech

title: Operator continuous with range in weak topology iff continuous with range in the norm topology
text:
I'm self studying MacCluer's book Elementary Functional Analysis, and I came across the following problem.

Problem 3.18.
Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed linear spaces and suppose $T \colon X \to Y$ is linear.
Show that $T$ is continuous if $\varphi \circ T$ is continuous for all $\varphi$ in $X^*$.

Firstly, I think there is a typo in that the author meant $Y^*$ instead of $X^*$. One can then rephrase the problem as saying that $T$ is continuous with $Y$ having the norm topology if $T$ is continuous with $Y$ having the weak topology. (Note that the converse is straightforward, so we can also rephrase the problem as iff.)
But I was not able to prove the result unless I assumed Y is Banach. Assuming this, then we know that if $T$ is unbounded, then $TB_1$ is not bounded, where $B_1$ is the unit ball in $X$. Then one shows through the uniform boundedness principle that there will exist some $\varphi \in Y^*$ such that $\varphi(TB_1)$ is unbounded, completing the proof.
Is it true that we need $Y$ to be Banach, meaning that the author has made two typos in a single question? Also, what is the intuition for this result that two different topologies on $Y$ pick out the same set of continuous functions?

title: Is the set of $L^2([0,1])$ functions $g$ s.t. $g\circ \psi = f\circ \phi$ for fixed $f\in L^2$ and some $\phi_*(dx)=dx, \psi_*(dx)=dx$ closed?
text:
Consider the $L^2$ space for the Lebesgue measure $dx$, i.e., the set of functions $f:[0,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\int_{0}^{1}|f(x)|^2dx<\infty$. Fix one function $f\in L^2$ and the space of $dx$-invariant transforms $\textrm{Inv}(dx)$ i.e. the set of measurable functions $\phi:[0,1]\to [0,1]$ such that $\phi_* dx = dx$. Here, $\phi_* \mu$ where $\mu$ is a measure represents the pushforward of a measure defined by $\phi_* \mu(A)=\mu(\phi^{-1}(A))$.
We can define a subset of $L^2$ by $[f] = \{g\in L^2|\exists \phi, \psi \in \textrm{Inv}(dx) \textrm{ s.t. } g\circ \phi=f\circ \psi\}$. Now, the main question is as follows:
Question. Is $[f]$ closed in $L^2$?
Background. I am considering an action of a semigroup $\textrm{Inv}(dx)$ on $L^2$ by $g\circ \phi$ for $g\in L^2,\phi\in \textrm{Inv}(dx)$. The relation $f\sim g\Leftrightarrow f\circ \phi =g\circ \psi$ for some $\phi,\psi  \in \textrm{Inv}(dx)$ defines an equivalence relation, and to see topological properties of the quotient space $L^2/\textrm{Inv}(dx)$, I want to investigate the closedness of $[f]$. For example, the closed and another condition implies the quotient is complete; see here.
My attempt. To start, I considered a trivial case where $f(x)=0$. Then $[0]=\{g\in L^2|\exists \phi,\psi\in \textrm{Inv}(dx) \textrm{ s.t. }g\circ \phi = 0\}$. I think a function like $\phi(x)=x$ for $x\in (0,1]$ but $\phi(0)=1$ should preserve $dx$ since leaving out a few points should not affect the measure. So I am guessing that $[0]$ is the set of functions that are zero almost everywhere, but in $L^2$ space, such functions are identified as $f(x)=0$ anyway, so in that sense, we should have $[0]=\{0\}$, which is closed.
However, this is a very hand-wavy argument that I do not know how to make it rigorous. Moreover, this only covers the trivial situation and considering general functions seems hard.
author: Kaira

title: $24$ meteorites reach the Earth's surface each year. Prob. that no more than $3$ such meteorites will come in one month. Solution verification.
text:
An average of $24$ meteorites of a fixed size reach the Earth's surface each year. Determine the approximate probability that no more than 3 such meteorites will arrive in September 2028.

Given that an average of $24$ meteors hit the Earth per year, we can find the monthly average by dividing by $12$: $\lambda = \frac{24}{12} = 2 \ (\text{meteors per month})$
The Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda = 2$ describes the probability of $k$ events (meteors) occurring in a fixed interval (one month):
$$P(X=k)= \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$$
We need to calculate: $\mathbb{P}(X \leq 3) = \mathbb{P}(X=0) + \mathbb{P}(X=1) + \mathbb{P}(X=2) + \mathbb{P}(X=3)$ where:

$\mathbb{P}(X=0) = e^{-2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X=1) = 2e^{-2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X=2) = 2e^{-2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X=3) = \frac{4e^{-2}}{3}$

Therefore, the probability is equal to:
$$\mathbb{P}(X \leq 3) = 1 - e^{-2} - 2e^{-2} - 2e^{-2} - \frac{4e^{-2}}{3} = \frac{19}{3} e^{-2}$$
Is that correct?

title: Dimension of some subspace of real polynomials of degree $\leq n$
text:
I am now a little confused about the Question 14 from section 1.10 in Calculus Volume II by Tom Apostol, which states that

Let $P_{n}$ denote the linear space of all real polynomials of degree $\leq n$, where $n$ is fixed, let $S$ denote the set of all polynomials $f$ in $P_{n}$ satisfying the following differential equation $$f(0)+f'(0) = 0$$ Determine whether $S$ is a subspace of $P_{n}$ and the dimension of $S$ if it is a subspace.

I've proved that this $S$ is indeed a subspace and try to determine its dimension, if we solved the differential equation above, it implies that $c_{1}+c_{0} = 0$ if $f$ is a polynomial of degree $k\leq n$ of the form $f = \sum_{i=0}^{k}c_{i}x^{i}$. Now I have two potential answers, and I hope someone can help me figure out which one is correct.
The first answer is $n+1$. This is because we need the basis ${1,x,x^{2},\cdots,x^{n}}$ to span this subspace. For instance, $x-1$ is a solution to the DE above and we need the linear combination of $1$ and $x$ to form this solution.
The second answer is $n$. The reason for this is that after we solved the DE above, it imposes a restriction on $c_{0}$ and $c_{1}$. More specifically, now we only need $n$ coefficients to determine a certain solution.
Now I think the first one is correct, because it fits the definition of a basis. For the second answer, I think it already implicitly assumed the $n+1$ basis and confused the definition of dimension and degree of freedom, but I am not very sure about this.
author: John

title: Placing triangles around a central triangle: Optimal Strategy?
text:
Now cross-posted to MathOverflow (link).


Question: There is an equilateral triangle. Two players alternate turns placing non-overlapping equilateral triangles of the same size that touch the original one; contact needs to exist for at least one point. When a player cannot make such a placement, they lose. Which player has an optimal strategy, and what is it?

This question is a variation on the classic one about placing circles around an initial circle (for which player two wins e.g. using a mirroring strategy). The game is similarly solvable for a square.
The maximum number of equilateral triangles of the same size that can touch a single equilateral triangle of that size is twelve (alternatively phrased, the kissing number of an equilateral triangle is $12$). For this reason, the game ends after finitely many moves; in particular, it will be done within twelve moves. Therefore, one of the two players has an optimal strategy. What is it?
If this has been studied elsewhere – or already posed on MSE! – then please alert me. (My searches produced nothing.)
One of the principal difficulties appears to be a lack of exploitable symmetry. Given the solid black equilateral triangle to begin the game as below, suppose player one (blue) moves as follows:

Initially, one might believe that player two's moves can now be reflected using some sort of mirror symmetry. However, player two (red) can now win the game as follows:

From this arrangement, we see that blue's subsequent moves can be mirrored by red, which means red cannot encounter an impossible placement unless blue did in the previous turn. Thus, we detect one strategy that is not optimal for player one. But I do not see a clear generalization or next step around how to form an optimal strategy for either player.
author: Benjamin Dickman

title: One journalist makes $2$ typos per article, second $3.2$ and third $4$. Prob. that a random article contains at least 2 typos. Solution verification.
text:
The newspaper employs three journalists: A, B and C.
A makes an average of $2$ typos per article, for B and C the averages are $3.2$ and $4$, respectively.
The Monday edition of the newspaper contains fifteen articles:

$4$, written by A,
$5$, written by B,
$6$, written by C.

Calculate the probability that a randomly selected article from this issue contains at least two typos.

I think that we can model the number of typos in an article using the Poisson distribution.

A: $\lambda_1=2$ typos per article
B: $\lambda_2=3.2$ typos per article
C: $\lambda_3=4$ typos per article

Probability of an Article from Each Journalist:

$\mathbb{P}(\text{article was written by A}) = \frac{4}{15}$
$\mathbb{P}(\text{article was written by B}) = \frac{5}{15}$
$\mathbb{P}(\text{article was written by C}) = \frac{6}{15}$

For a Poisson-distributed random variable $X$ with rate $λ$, the probability of $X=k$ typos is:
$$\mathbb{P}(X=k)= \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$$
We need to calculate $\mathbb{P}(X \geq 2)$ for each journalist:
$$\mathbb{P}(X \geq 2) = 1 − \mathbb{P}(X=0) − \mathbb{P}(X=1)$$
For A:

$\mathbb{P}(X_1​ = 0) = e^{-2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X_1 ​= 1) = 2e^{-2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X_1​ \geq 2) = 1 − e^{−2} −2e^{−2} = 1−3e^{−2}$

For B:

$\mathbb{P}(X2​=0) = e^{-3.2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X2​=0) = 3.2e^{-3.2}$
$\mathbb{P}(X_1​ \geq 2) = 1 − e^{-3.2} − 3.2e^{-3.2} = 1 − 4.2e^{−3.2}$

For C:

$\mathbb{P}(X3​=0) = e^{-4}$
$\mathbb{P}(X3​=1) = 4e^{-4}$
$\mathbb{P}(X3​≥2) = 1 − e^{−4} − 4e^{−4} = 1 − 5e^{−4}$

Therefore the probability is equal to:
$$\frac{4}{15}(1−3e^{−2}) + \frac{5}{15}(1 − 4.2e^{−3.2}) + \frac{6}{15}(1 − 5e^{−4})$$
Is that correct?

title: Trouble with proof that $L^p(\mathbb R ^n)$ is separable
text:
I'm having trouble understanding the following proof from Linear Functional Analysis - An Application-Oriented Introduction (4.18, Proof for (4)):
Let $\epsilon>0, 0<p<\infty$ and $f\in L^p(\mathbb R ^n)$. Let further
$$
Q_\epsilon(z) := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n ; z_i \leq x_i \leq z_i + \epsilon \ \text{for} \ i = 1, \ldots, n \} \ \text{for} \ z \in \epsilon \mathbb{Z}^n
$$
We define the piecewise constant interpolation $f_\epsilon$ as:
$$
f_\epsilon(x) := \sum_{z \in \epsilon \mathbb{Z}^n} \chi_{Q_\epsilon(z)}(x) \alpha_{\epsilon, z}, \ \ \alpha_{\epsilon, z} := \frac{1}{\epsilon^n} \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} f(y) \, dy
$$
This interpolant approximates $f$, since:
$$
\begin{align}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |f_\epsilon(x) - f(x)|^p \, dx & = \sum_z \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} |\alpha_{\epsilon, z} - f(x)|^p \, dx\\
& = \sum_z \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} \left| \frac{1}{\epsilon^n} \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} (f(y) - f(x)) \, dy \right|^p \, dx \label{1}\tag{1}\\
& = \sum_z \frac{1}{\epsilon^n} \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} \int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} |f(y) - f(x)|^p \, dy \, dx\label{2}\tag{2}\\
& \leq \sup_{h : |h| \leq \epsilon} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |f(y + h) - f(y)|^p \, dy = \sup_{h : |h| \leq \epsilon} \| f(\cdot + h) - f \|_{L^p}^p.\label{3}\tag{3}
\end{align}
$$

I'm honestly totally lost: In \eqref{1} for example, I don't see how we can factor out $\frac{1}{\epsilon^n}$ like that. I tried doing it step by step, but I get:
$$
\begin{align}
\sum_{z}\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}\left|\alpha_{\epsilon,z}-f(x)\right|^p\, dx
& =\sum_{z}\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}\Bigg|\bigg(\frac{1}{\epsilon^n}\underbrace{\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)} f(y)\, d y}_{=:u}\bigg)-f(x)\Bigg|^p\, dx
\\
& =\sum_{z}\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}\left|\frac{1}{\epsilon^n}\left(u-\epsilon^nf(x)\right)\right|^p\, dx
\\
& =\frac{1}{\epsilon^n}\sum_{z}\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}\left|u-\epsilon^nf(x)\right|^p\, dx
\\
& =\frac{1}{\epsilon^n}\sum_{z}\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}\left|\int_{Q_\epsilon(z)}{f(y)-\epsilon^nf(x)}\, d y\right|^p\, dx
\end{align}
$$
But for $\epsilon\neq 1$ this seems distinct from \eqref{2}.
For \eqref{2} I do not understand why we have an equality, and why it holds for all $p$. I could get an inequality $\le$ since for any function $g$ we have $\left|\int_{\Omega} gd\mu\right|\le\int_{\Omega}\left|g\right|d\mu$ and we maybe can fit Jensen's inequality, but that'd only give an inequality?
author: ConnFus

title: Sangaku problem: Show that five circles have equal radii.
text:
Inspired by Sangaku problems such as these, I created the following Sangaku problem.

Consider the following diagram.

Description: The diagram shows the circle $x^2+y^2=1$, two red chords with equations $y=\pm mx+k$ where $m>1$ and $0<k<1$, and two green chords that each meet one of the red chords on the circle below $y=0$ and is perpendicular to the other red chord. The values $m$ and $k$ are chosen so that there exist two blue circles inside the unit circle that are reflections in the $y$-axis, the left of which is tangent to: the unit circle, the chord $y=mx+k$ at the midpoint of the chord $y=mx+k$, the chord $y=-mx+k$, and the chord perpendicular to $y=mx+k$.
Inscribe five orange circles as shown below. (The orange circles are inscribed in every previously unoccupied region except the two triangles.)


Show that the five orange circles have equal radii.

I have a computer-assisted solution. I am looking for a computer-free solution.

My computer-assisted solution
Define the following four points:

$(x_1,y_1)$: Point where the right blue circle touches the chord $y=-mx+k$.
$(x_2,y_2)$: Point where the right blue circle touches the unit circle
$(x_3,y_3)$: Centre of the right blue circle
$(x_4,y_4)$: Lower-left point where the chord $y=mx+k$ meets the unit circle

$x_1$ is the average of the sum of roots of $x^2+(-mx+k)^2=1$, so $x_1=\frac{mk}{1+m^2}$ and $y_1=\frac{-m^2k}{1+m^2}+k$.
$x_2$ is the larger root of $x^2+\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)^2=1$, so $x_2=\frac{m}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}$ and $y_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}$.
$x_3=\frac12(x_1+x_2)=\frac12\left(\frac{mk+m\sqrt{1+m^2}}{1+m^2}\right)$ and $y_3=\frac12\left(\frac{k+\sqrt{1+m^2}}{1+m^2}\right)$.
The distance from $(x_3,y_3)$ to the chord $y=mx+k$ equals the radius of the right blue circle, which is $R=\frac12\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}$. This gives one equation with $m$ and $k$.
$x_4$ is the smaller root of $x^2+(mx+k)^2=1$, so $x_4=\frac{-mk-\sqrt{1+m^2-k^2}}{1+m^2}$ and $y_4=\frac{-m^2k-m\sqrt{1+m^2-k^2}}{1+m^2}+k$. The centre of the right blue circle, $(x_3,y_3)$, lies on the line that passes through $(x_4,y_4)$ with gradient $1$. This gives another equation with $m$ and $k$.
With help from Wolfram, I solved these two equations to get an approximation of $m$, then put this approximation back into Wolfram, which suggested it is the real root of a certain cubic polynomial. Using this method, I got:

$3m^3-6m^2+3m-4=0\implies m\approx1.8491482$
$17k^3-33k^2+30k-6=0\implies k\approx0.2681854$
$17R^3-54R^2+57R-16=0\implies R\approx0.4362138$ ($R=$ radius of blue circles)

Let $S$ be the radius of the orange circle nearest the centre of the unit circle. It is easy to show that $\frac{R}{S}=m$ (note that the obtuse angle between the green chords equals the obtuse angle between the red chords, then compare the central orange circle and a blue circle). Again with the help of Wolfram, this gives:

$17S^3-30S^2+57S-12=0\implies S\approx 0.2358999$

Assuming that the five orange circles have equal radii, I used the closed forms for $m,k,R,S$ to make a desmos graph of the diagram, and all the circles and chords fit together perfectly.

Fun fact: The centres of the top four circles are the vertices of a square.

This comes from the fact that the distance from the centre of the top orange circle to the intersection of the red chords, which is $1-S-k$, equals $x_3$.
(Other Sangaku problems that I created are here and here.)

title: Generalization to Rauch's comparison theorem
text:
I was trying to do an exercise of proving that a geodesic of length greater than $\pi$, in a manifold of sectional curvature greater or equal to $1$, has a conjugate point of multiplicity at least $n-1$, where $n$ is the dimension of the manifold and by "multiplicity" I mean the Morse index of the geodesic.

author: Enio de Sousa Santos

title: Eigenvalues of a circulant matrix
text:
So we define a circulant matrix as follows. Let the first column be $$a^t = [a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots,a_{n-1}].$$ The other entries are given by circularly permuting the column 1. For example column 2 is given as transpose of $[a_{n-1}, a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n-2}]$.
Let $S_n$ be the set of $n$-periodic sequences. Let $AX = Y$ be a matrix equation where $A$ is circulant.
Let $$\tilde{x},\tilde{y}$$ be the natural extensions of $X$ and $Y$ to sequences in $S_n$.
I have shown the above matrix equation is equivalent to $$[a*\tilde{x}] = \tilde{y}$$
where $a$ is the first column of $A$ and $*$ denotes the convolution of two sequences in $S_n$.
We now claim the eigenvalues of $A$ are exactly the elements in the discrete fourier transform $F[a]$ where $a$ is seen as an element in $S_n$.
One direction is easy to show. You basically see that if $$AX = \lambda X$$ then this to say that $$a*\tilde{x} = \lambda\tilde{x}$$ Doing a DFT on both sides and using the convolution theorem then gives $$F[a]_kF[\tilde{x}]_k = \lambda F[\tilde{x}]_k.$$ This shows basically every eigenvalue is an entry in $F[a]$.
How do we prove the converse? I feel I am missing something obvious but it is what it is.

title: Proving Mutual Absolute Continuity of two Haar Measures

title: Spivak Exercise, Prove Vandermonde's Identity $\sum_{k=0}^{l}\binom{n}{k}\binom{m}{l-k}=\binom{n+m}{l}$
text:
Prove that
$$\sum_{k=0}^{l}\binom{n}{k}\binom{m}{l-k}=\binom{n+m}{l}$$

Hint: Apply the binomial theorem to $(1+x)^n(1+x)^m$

Proof:
Following Spivak's advice, we have
$\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k=(1+x)^n$ and $\sum_{j=0}^{m}\binom{m}{j}x^j=(1+x)^m$
Since $(1+x)^n(1+x)^m=(1+x)^{n+m}$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k\cdot \sum_{j=0}^{m}\binom{m}{j}x^j=\sum_{(j+k)=0}^{n+m}\binom{n+m}{j+k}x^{j+k}$$
Which is the sum of all numbers in the form $\left\langle \binom{n}{k}x^k \cdot\binom{m}{j}x^j \right\rangle$ At this point we should realize that $\binom{n+m}{l}$ represents the coefficient for $x^l$. So we only care about terms of the l'th order so we make the restriction that $j+k=l$. In other words we want the sum of all the numbers in the form$\left\langle \binom{n}{k}x^k \cdot\binom{m}{l-k}x^{l-k} \right\rangle$ .
$$(\sum_{k=0}^{l}\binom{n}{k}\binom{m}{l-k})x^l=\binom{n+m}{l}x^l$$
Q.E.D

title: Equivalent characterizations of a Poisson process
text:
Consider a counting process $N(t)$, and the following three conditions that I believe are equivalent:
$$
\begin{aligned}
(A) \quad& N(t) \text{ is a Poisson process of intensity }λ \\
(B) \quad& V(t) = N(t)-λt \text{ is a martingale} \\
(C) \quad& W(t) = \exp[-θN(t)+λt(1-e^{-θ})] \text{ is a martingale for all } θ
\end{aligned}
$$
It’s straightforward to show $(A)\implies (B)$, and $(A)\implies (C)$. The direction $(B)\implies (A)$ is Watanabe’s martingale characterization of a Poisson process, see this question. The direction $(C)\implies (A)$ is covered in e.g. [1, 12.7.9, p.565]. Therefore clearly $(B)\implies (A) \implies (C)$.
Question: Is there a direct connection that shows $(B)\implies (C)$, i.e. using the martingale property of $V(t)$ to show that $W(t)$ is a martingale for any choice of $θ$?

[1] Grimmett, Geoffrey, and David Stirzaker. Probability and random processes. Oxford university press, 2020.

I find that

How can such a complicated looking integral have such a simple solution? The problem is essentially a calculation of the work required to inflate a soap bubble.

title: Square root definition
text:
Perhaps this is silly, but here it is:
If we search for the square root definition it goes as follows (taken from Wikipedia):
"In mathematics, a square root of a number $x$ is a number $y$ such that $y^2$; in other words, a number y whose square (the result of multiplying the number by itself, or $y\times y$) is $x$.
For example, 4 and −4 are square roots of $16$ because $4^2=(-4)^2 = 16$."
At the same time, if we look at the definition of the square root of a number squared, we get $f(x) = \sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x \rvert$.
These are totally fine and I know how to use them properly. But at the same time, we have one single function with seemingly two different definitions depending on which operand it operates on; in one of them we make use of the absolute value function, on the other we don't.
I'm not saying (obviously) that these are wrong or inconsistent, but would it make any sense (or perhaps be more elegant), if we simply defined the square root of a positive real number (squared or not) using the absolute value function, as something like:
$$f(x) = \sqrt{x} = \lvert y \rvert, \iff y^2 = x$$
?
Thank you,
All the best!

title: Number of copies of a fundamental domain for $\Gamma_0(q)/\{\pm1\} $ needed to cover a region $P(Y) = \{z \mid \Im z > Y, \Re(z) \in ]0,1] \}$ ($Y>0$)
text:
I've been struggling on a claim in W.Duke's paper on the dimension of the space of cusp forms of weight one (see : https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9411212 Lemma 2 p.5).
Take a cuspidal form $f \in \mathcal{S}_1(\Gamma_0(q))$ and let $D$ be a fundamental domain for $\Gamma_0(q)$. The goal is to get an upper-bound on the following integral :
$$I_Y :=\int_{P(Y)} |f(z)|^2y^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y$$
in terms of the Petersson inner product $\langle f,f \rangle$ and where $P(Y)$ is the region afore-defined. Let me explain what I've already figured out for myself.
By noting that the integrand is the actual expression of the Petersson inner product for weight 1 forms, having a finite covering $P(Y) \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^{r_Y} g_i D$ for some $g_i$'s in $\Gamma_0(q)/\{\pm1\}$ would yield the following :
$$I_Y \leq r_Y \langle f, f \rangle$$
It then boils down to finding $g_i's$ or at least give an upper-bound on $r_Y$. Duke's claim (Lemma 2 p.5  (8)) is that :
$$I_Y \leq \max_{z \in P(Y)} \sharp\{g \in \Gamma_0(q)/\{\pm1\} \mid gz \in P(Y) \} \langle f,f\rangle$$
This is where I'd need some help. Let's call the max in the previous inequality $A$. Note that it follows from the rest of Duke's proof that this $A$ is finite.
If I take some arbitrary $z \in P(Y)$, then the size of the orbit of $\Gamma_0(q)z$ that lies within $P(Y)$ must be at most $A$. Should the integral be a finite sum then one could argue "points in the same orbit appear at most $A$ times hence the inequality" but that is obviously not true here. To get such a bound it seems to me that we would need some statement along these lines :
Take any $z$ in $P(Y)$, if $G_z := \{g \in \Gamma_0(q)/ \{\pm 1\} \mid gz \in P(Y)\}$ then one has a covering $$P(Y) \subset \bigcup_{g \in G_z} gD$$
Now, is that even true ? Or how does Duke's argument even work? I've tried to solve this a couple of times and also asked my supervisor but we couldn't get past it so if anyone knows the exact argument I'm all ears.

I'm unsure if we need condition (C) for the lemma itself to hold or if we need some more relaxed condition. In either case, I don't know how to make progress on the Lemma even if I assume condition (C).

title: integration by parts $\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} -\Delta u (u-M)\varphi dx$
text:
I'm trying to understand how it integrates by parts the following integral. This belong to the academic paper Stable solutions of $-\Delta u=f(u)$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with DOI 10.4171/JEMS/217. Specifically, page 863.
Proof of Theorem 1.1. For $R>0$, let $B_R$ denote the ball of radius $R$ centred at the origin. We begin by proving that there exists a constant $C>0$ independent of $R>0$ such that
$$
\int_{B_R}|\nabla u|^2 d x \leq C R^{N-2} .
$$
Let $M \geq\|u\|_{\infty}, \varphi \in C_c^2\left(\mathbb{R}^N\right)$ and multiply (1) by $(u-M) \varphi$ :
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}-\Delta u(u-M) \varphi d x=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} f(u)(u-M) \varphi d x .
$$
Integrating by parts and recalling that $f \geq 0$, it follows that
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2 \varphi d x+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(u-M) \nabla u \nabla \varphi d x=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} f(u)(u-M) \varphi d x \leq 0,
$$
whence
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\nabla u|^2 \varphi d x & \leq-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{1}{2} \nabla(u-M)^2 \nabla \varphi d x=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{(u-M)^2}{2} \Delta \varphi d x \\
& \leq 2 M^2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\Delta \varphi| d x .
\end{aligned}
$$

title: How to accurately average a function with a nonlinear response?

I am a physics PhD student working in optics and I have a bit of a weird problem that I am trying to sort out and I'm hoping you math folks can help me with.
Without boring you with the experimental details, I have a laser, characterized by its pulse energy, which I shine onto a detector which then outputs a voltage in response to the pulse energy. The pulse energy has some coefficient of variation (also known as normalized root-mean-square deviation, percent RMS, or relative standard deviation) and for my purposes this value is usually around $10\%$. Normally this isn't a problem, but for the specific sensor I am working with and interested in using, I want to characterize it's nonlinear response to this pulse energy.
Theoretically, the sensor signal should roughly follow the equation Signal $= E^n$, where $n \in \mathbb{R}$ is greater than $1$, and $E$ is the pulse energy. This value of $n$ is supposed to correspond to the ratio of the bandgap energy of the sensor and the photon energy of the laser being used, but due to some physics which I won't detail here, we believe that for longer wavelengths (smaller values of the photon energy) this relationship will no longer hold and will be begin to decrease.
As a concrete example:

For $\lambda = 2um, n \sim 2$


For $\lambda = 4um, n \sim 4$


For $\lambda = 8um, n \sim 6$

That is to say, the nonlinear scaling begins to break-down at longer wavelengths.
So on to my actual question: Due to the fluctuations in my pulse energy, it is necessary that I average the response from my detector over many pulses, but since the detector has a nonlinear response, will a simple time-average actually give me a representative answer or will it give me garbage?
My intuition is that it will give me garbage because a pulse with energy $10\%$ greater than the average will contribute a signal proportional to $1.1^n$ while a pulse with energy $10\%$ smaller than average will contribute a signal proportional to $0.9^n$.
How should I go about averaging this sort of nonlinear response when I have uncertainty in the input variable as well? Is there a form of "nonlinear averaging" that applies here? Any suggestions for textbooks/papers that would explain how to do this in a relatively straightforward manner?

title: Correspondence between sheaves of ideals and closed immersion
text:
Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a locally ringed space.
Let $\mathcal J$ be a sheaf of ideals over $\mathcal O_X$. Then we can construct a closed immersion of locally ringed spaces: $$(Z(\mathcal J),i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J))\xrightarrow{(i,i^\#)} (X,\mathcal O_X),$$ where $Z(\mathcal J)\subset X$ is the set of $x\in X$ such that $\mathcal J_x\subsetneq \mathcal O_{X,x}$, which is closed, and $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion.
If we take $\operatorname{ker}i^\#$, do we get back $\mathcal J$? I think no because for example, if $X$ is an affine scheme, the kernel of any closed immersion into $X$ is quasi-coherent, so if we choose $\mathcal J$ not quasi-coherent, we surely do not get it back.
Hence I wanted to ask: is $\operatorname{ker}i^\#$ in general obtained by $\mathcal J$ via some canonical construction?
Edit after answer. Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a locally ringed space, and let $\mathcal J$ be a sheaf of ideals over $\mathcal O_X$. There is a canonical morphism of ring sheaves $i^\#:\mathcal O_X\to i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)$, where $i:Z(\mathcal J)\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion defined above.
We want to prove that $\operatorname {ker}i^\#=\mathcal J$ by proving that they are equal on the stalks, so let's compute $(\operatorname {ker}i^\#)_x=\operatorname {ker}(i^\#_x)$ at any $x\in X$.
Suppose first that $x\in Z(\mathcal J)$. Look at the canonical map: $$\mathcal O_{X,x}\to i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x\to i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x$$ the first map $i^\#_x$ factors as: $$\mathcal O_{X,x}\to(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x\to i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x$$ and we know that the composition: $$(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x\to i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x\to i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x$$ is just the canonical isomorphism. Moreover since $i$ is an immersion we have that $i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x\to i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x$ is an isomorphism, proving that $\operatorname {ker}(i^\#_x)=\mathcal J_x$.
If instead $x\in X\setminus Z(\mathcal J)$, we know that $\mathcal J_x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, and $i_*i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal J)_x=0$, so automatically $\operatorname{ker}(i^\#_x)=\mathcal O_{X,x}$.
Thus since $\operatorname{ker}(i^\#_x)$ and $\mathcal J_x$ coincide as ideals of =$\mathcal O_{X,x}$ for all $x\in X$, we conclude that they coincide as sheaves of ideals.

title: Conjugate of a Gel'fand pattern
text:
Background:
A Gel'fand pattern is a set of numbers
$$
\left[\begin{array}{}
\lambda_{1,n} &      & \lambda_{2,n} &        &        & \dots  &        & &  \lambda_{n-1,n} &             & \lambda_{n,n} \\
             & \lambda_{1,n-1} &   & \lambda_{2,n-1} &        &    \dots     & &  \lambda_{n-2,n-1} &           & \lambda_{n-1,n-1} \\
             &      &        &     &        & \dots  \\
             &      &        &     & \lambda_{1,2} &  & \lambda_{2,2} \\   
             &      &        &     &        & \lambda_{1,1}
\end{array}\right]
$$
which satisfy the "betweenness condition" $\lambda_{i,j+1} \geq \lambda_{i+j,j+1} \geq \lambda_{ij}$, i.e., that each number has to be (weakly) between the two numbers above it.
Gel'fand patterns can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with Young tableaux, where each row corresponds to the shape of the Young diagram for the first $j$ particles. For example:
$$
\begin{align}
\begin{matrix}
1 & 2 & 5 \\
3 &   &   \\
4
\end{matrix}
&\longleftrightarrow&
\begin{bmatrix}
3 && 1 && 1 && 0 && 0 \\
& 2 && 1 && 1 && 0 &  \\
&& 2 && 1 && 0 &&     \\
&&& 2 && 0 &&&        \\
&&&& 1 &&&&           \\
\end{bmatrix}
\\
\begin{matrix}
1 & 3 & \\
2 & 5 & \\
4 &   &
\end{matrix}
&\longleftrightarrow&
\begin{bmatrix}
2 && 2 && 1 && 0 && 0 \\
& 2 && 1 && 1 && 0 &  \\
&& 2 && 1 && 0 &&     \\
&&& 1 && 1 &&&        \\
&&&& 1 &&&&           \\
\end{bmatrix}
\end{align}
$$
Question:
Is there a closed-form way of finding the "conjugate" of a Gel'fand pattern? That is, knowing the $\lambda_{i,j}$, can I calculate $\tilde{\lambda}_{ij}$? For Young tableaux, one can obtain the conjugate by reflecting across the diagonal. The conjugates for the examples would be
$$
\begin{align}
\begin{matrix}
1 & 3 & 4 \\
2 &   &   \\
5
\end{matrix}
&\longleftrightarrow&
\begin{bmatrix}
3 && 1 && 1 && 0 && 0 \\
& 3 && 1 && 0 && 0 &  \\
&& 2 && 1 && 0 &&     \\
&&& 1 && 1 &&&        \\
&&&& 1 &&&&           \\
\end{bmatrix}
\\
\begin{matrix}
1 & 2 & 4 \\
3 & 5
\end{matrix}
&\longleftrightarrow&
\begin{bmatrix}
3 && 2 && 0 && 0 && 0 \\
& 3 && 1 && 0 && 0 &  \\
&& 2 && 1 && 0 &&     \\
&&& 2 && 0 &&&        \\
&&&& 1 &&&&           \\
\end{bmatrix}
\end{align}
$$

Lemma Let $f$ be an absolutely continuous real-valued function on $[a, b ]$. If $f' = 0$ a.e. on $[a, b]$ then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.
Proof To show that $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$ we show that for every $c\in (a, b]$ we have
$f(c) = f(a)$. Now since $f' = 0$ a.e. on $[a, b]$, we have $f' = 0$ a.e. on $(a, c)$. Thus there
exists a null set $F\in(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}), \lambda)$ contained in $(a, c)$ such that $f' = 0$ on $E= (a, c)\setminus F$.
We have $E\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}) $ with $\lambda(E)=\lambda((a,c))=c-a<\infty.$.
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\eta>0$ be arbitrarily given. Let $\delta>0$ be a positive number corresponding to our $\varepsilon>0$ in the definition for the absolute continuity of $f$ on $[a,c]$. Now, at every $x\in E$ we have that $f'(x)=0$ so that there exists $h_x>0$ such that $$\lvert f(x+h)-f(x)<\eta h\quad\text{for every}\quad h\in (0,h_x).$$ Then the collection of closed intervals $$\mathcal{B}=\{[x, x+h]\; :\; h\in (0, h_x), x\in E\}$$ is a Vitali cover of $E$. Since $\mu(E)<\infty$ by the Vitali Covering Theorem there exists a finite disjoint subcollection $\{I_k\; |\: k=1,\dots, N\}$ of $\mathcal{B}$ such that $$\lambda\left( E\setminus \bigcup_{k=1}^N I_k\right)<\delta\tag1.$$ For each $x\in E$ let $h_x>0$ be chosen so small that $x+h_x<c$. Let $I_k=[x_k, y_k]$ with $x_k\in E\subset (a,b)$ for $k=1,\dots, N$ and let $\{I_k\;|\; k=1,\dots, N\}$ be so numbered that $$y_0:=a<x_1<y_1<x_2<y_2<\cdots < x_N<y_N<c:=x_{N+1}.$$ Since $E\subset (a,c)$ and $\lambda(E)=\lambda((a,b))$, $(1)$ implies that $$\lambda\left((a,c)\setminus \bigcup_{k=1}^N I_k\right)<\delta\tag2$$

Question. How can I get $(2)$?

From $(1)$ it is possible to obtain that $$\lambda((a,c))=\lambda(E)<\delta+\lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^N I_k\right)$$
But I can't understand why the fact that $E\subset (a,b)$ can help us. Can anyone give me some hits?

title: Why is there no logarithmic form of the exponential distributive rule/power of a product rule?
text:
When learning the laws of exponents and logarithms, one finds that there is a correspondence. Each law of exponents has a corresponding equivalent expression in terms of logarithms. For example, the exponential of a sum law, $a^{x+y}=a^xa^y$ becomes $\log(wz)=\log w + \log z$ after you take a logarithm and relabel. Or in words, since exponentials turn sums into products, their inverse function must turn products into sums. The Repeated exponentiation law $(a^x)^y=a^{xy}$ becomes $\log z^y = y\log z$.
If you make a list of all the rules of exponents, you'll find that all of them (with one exception) has a useful form expressed in terms of logarithms. Personally I find understanding this relationship between the two sets of identities to be the best way to learn them, remember them, and teach them.
However there is one law, which may be called the distributive law for exponentiation, or the power of a product law, namely $(ab)^x=a^xb^x,$ for which there seems to be no useful logarithmic version. My question is, why not? I can see that because it involves exponentiation operations with three different bases, if there were a logarithmic identity it would awkwardly involve different logarithm bases. But is there more we can say?

title: Geometric fixed-points of MO
text:
Recall that the value of the orthogonal spectrum $\mathbf{MO}$ at an inner product space $V$ is the Thom space of the tautological bundle over the Grassmannian of $|V|$-demensiomal planes in $V\oplus V$:
$$\mathbf{MO}(V) = \text{Th}\left(\text{Gr}_{|V|}(V\oplus V)\right)=\{(x, U) \subset (V\oplus V) \times \text{Gr}_{|V|}(V\oplus V) : x \in U\} \cup \{\infty\}.$$
The structure maps are given by
$$\sigma_{V,W}: S^V \wedge \mathbf{MO}(W) \longrightarrow  \mathbf{MO}(V\oplus W), \quad \quad v \wedge (x, U) \longmapsto \bigg(\kappa_{V, W}\big(\underbrace{(v,0)}_{\in V\oplus V}, \ \underbrace{x}_{\in W\oplus W}\big), \kappa_{V, W}\big(\underbrace{(V\oplus 0)}_{\subseteq V\oplus V}\oplus\underbrace{U}_{\subseteq W\oplus W}\big) \bigg)$$
where
$$\kappa_{V, W}: V\oplus V  \oplus W \oplus W \longrightarrow V\oplus W \oplus V \oplus W, \quad \quad \quad (v,v',w,w')\longmapsto (v,w,v',w').$$
Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, $\mathcal{U}_G$ a fixed complete $G$-universe and $s(\mathcal{U}_G)$ the poset of finite dimensional subrepresentations of $\mathcal{U}_G$. I'm trying to calculate the geometric fixed-point homotopy groups of $\mathbf{MO}$, following Example 6.1.46 in Stefan Schwede's Global Homotopy Theory. By definition,
$$\Phi^G_0 (\mathbf{MO}) = \underset{s(\mathcal{U}_G)}{\text{colim}}\  \left[ S^{V^G}, \ \mathbf{MO}(V)^G\right]_*$$
For a $G$-representation $W$ we write $W^\perp$ for $W - W^G$, where the minus sign means orthogonal complement. From the canonical decomposition
$$ \text{Gr}_{n}(W)^G \cong \coprod_{k\geq 0} \text{Gr}_{k}(W^G) \times  \text{Gr}_{n-k}(W^\perp)^G$$
we obtain
$$ \text{Th}\left(\text{Gr}_{n}(W)\right)^G \cong \bigvee_{k \geq 0} \text{Th}\left(\text{Gr}_{k}(W^G)\right) \wedge \text{Gr}_{n-k}(W^\perp)^G_+.$$
Letting $W = V\oplus V$ we have
$$  \bigvee_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(V^G)\wedge \text{Gr}_{|V^\perp|+j}(V^\perp\oplus V^\perp)_+^G \cong \mathbf{MO}(V)^G,$$
where $\mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}$ is the orthogonal spectrum given by
$$\mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(U) = \text{Th}\left(\text{Gr}_{|U|+j}(U\oplus U)\right).$$
Finally,
$$\Phi^G_0(\mathbf{MO}) \cong \bigoplus_{j\in \mathbb{Z}} \underset{s(\mathcal{U}_G)}{\text{colim}}\  \left[ S^{V^G}, \quad \mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(V^G)\wedge \text{Gr}_{|V^\perp|+j}(V^\perp\oplus V^\perp)_+^G\right]_*, \tag{1}\label{1}$$
where the stabilization map for $V \subseteq W \subseteq \mathcal{U}_G$ is given by sending a class represented by
$$f: S^{V^G} \longrightarrow \mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(V^G)\wedge \text{Gr}_{|V^\perp|+j}(V^\perp\oplus V^\perp)_+^G$$
to the composite
$$S^{W^G} \cong S^{(W-V)^G} \wedge S^{V^G} \xrightarrow{\text{id} \wedge f} S^{(W-V)^G}\wedge \mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(V^G)\wedge \text{Gr}_{|V^\perp|+j}(V^\perp\oplus V^\perp)_+^G \\ \xrightarrow{\sigma_{(W-V)^G, V^G} \wedge \text{incl}_{V, W}^j} \mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}(W^G)\wedge \text{Gr}_{|W^\perp|+j}(W^\perp\oplus W^\perp)_+^G$$
where
$$\text{incl}_{V, W}^j: \text{Gr}_{|V^\perp|+j}(V^\perp\oplus V^\perp)_+^G \longrightarrow \text{Gr}_{|W^\perp|+j}(W^\perp\oplus W^\perp)_+^G, \quad \quad L \longmapsto L + 0 \oplus\left( W^\perp - V^\perp\right).$$
My question is: What is the value of colimit \eqref{1} ? I'm hoping that it is the $\mathbf{MOP}^{[j]}$ homology of some Grassmannian, for example as in the case of $\mathbf{mO}$ in which we have
$$ \Phi^G_*(\mathbf{mO}) \cong \bigoplus_{j\geq 0}\mathbf{mO}_{*-j}\left(\text{Gr}_j(\mathcal{U}_G^\perp)^G\right).$$

title: Fundamental group of a smooth projective surface over $\mathbb{R}$.
text:
Let $X_{\mathbb{R}}$ be a smooth, projective surface over $\mathbb{R}$. Then its complexification, $X$, is a smooth complex projective surface.
$X_\mathbb{R}$ is a manifold, so we can talk about its pointed fundamental group, $\pi_1(X_\mathbb{R}, x)$, for a fixed $x\in X_{\mathbb{R}}$. On the other hand, it should be possible to define some sort of algebraic analog of $\pi_1(X_\mathbb{R})$, where one considers only loops given by intersections of $X_\mathbb{R}$ with algebraic curves in $X$.
Here's a first attempt to define such a group: Let
$\mathcal{C}$ be the collection of irreducible curves in $X$ passing through $x$. Then for each $\alpha \in \mathcal{C}$, $\alpha\cap X_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a finite union of curves in $X_{\mathbb{R}}$; let $\alpha_x$ denote the one passing through $x$. Let $$S = \{[\alpha_x] : \alpha\in\mathcal{C}\},$$ where $[\alpha_x]$ denotes the equivalence class of $\alpha_x$ up to pointed homotopy at $x$. Clearly, $S$ is a subset of $\pi_1(X, x)$. We let $\hat \pi_1(X, x)$ denote subgroup of $\pi_1(X, x)$ generated by $S$.
In some very simple cases, like $X = \mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}[i]\times \mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and $X_\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, we actually have $\hat \pi_1(X, x) = \pi_1(X, x)$. Indeed, the curves $\{x = 0\}, \{y = 0\}$ intersect $X_\mathbb{R}$ in loops generating $\pi_1(X_\mathbb{R})$. But this is a very simple case, and I'm wondering if one can expect these groups to be equal in general
Does this group $\hat \pi_1(X_\mathbb{R})$ have a name? It seems pretty natural, so I'd imagine it has been studied.
Any comments or pointers to references would be greatly appreciated!

Can we say that $G$ acts on $P$ via ANTI-equivariant diffeomorphisms if $f_g^\ast c_1(P)=-c_1(P)$?
We recall that $f:P\to P$ is equivariant if $f(e^{it}\cdot p)=e^{it}\cdot f(p)$ and anti-equivariant if $f(e^{it}\cdot p)=e^{-it}f(p)$.

The definition of $\psi$ implies

$$
and,

EOP. The questions here:

title: No Arbitrage iff no generalized Arbitrage
text:
Let’s consider a market in finite discrete time with trading dates $0,1,\dots,T$ probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, filtration $\{\mathcal{F_t}\}_{t \in \{0,1, \dots, T\}}$, $N$ traded assets, whose prices are described by a $\mathbb{R}^N$-valued stochastic-process $S=\{S_t\}_{t \in \{0,1, \dots, T\}}$ such that $\forall t: \ S_t^0>0$ a.s. (i.e. $S^0$ is a numéraire).
Now a strategy $\Psi=\{\Psi_t\}_{t \in \{1, \dots, T\}}$ is a $\mathbb{R}^N$-valued predictable process. It’s corresponding value process is $\tilde{V}(\Psi)=\{\tilde{V}_t(\Psi)\}_{t \in \{0,1, \dots, T\}}$, where $\tilde{V}_0(\Psi):=\Psi_1 \cdot S_0$ and $\tilde{V}_t(\Psi):=\Psi_t \cdot S_t$. We call the strategy it „self-financing“ if $\forall t<T: (\Psi_{t+1}-\Psi_t)\cdot S_t=0$. We call it „$a$-admissible“ if $\forall t: \tilde{V}_t(\Psi) >a$ a.s. and just „admissible“ is it is $a$-admissible for some $a$.
Now an arbitrage opportunity is a self-financing strategy $\Psi$ such that $\tilde{V}_0(\Psi)\leq 0$ a.s. and $\tilde{V}_T(\Psi)\geq 0$ a.s. and additionally either $\mathbb{P}(\tilde{V}_T(\Psi)> 0)>0$ or $\mathbb{P}(\tilde{V}_0(\Psi)< 0)>0$.
I am now supposed to show that in a market with numéraire there exist arbitrage opportunities if and only if there exist admissible arbitrage opportunities.
The strategy of the proof is probably to take an arbitrage opportunity $\Psi$ and from it construct another arbitrage opportunity $\Phi$ that is admissible. I tried various things, but didn’t succeed. I presume that we somehow must put more into the first component of $\Phi$, corresponding to the numéraire in order to make it admissible, while simultaneously making sure that it stays self-financing. I‘d be very happy if someone could give me some hints.

title: Generic hyperplane sections of an irreducible projective variety is irreducible
text:
I am reading Principles of Algebraic Geometry by Griffiths and Harris. They asserted that the generic hyperplane section $H\cap V$ of an irreducible nondegenerate variety $V$ of dimension $\geq 2$ is again irreducible.
The proof follows: pick a smooth point $p\in V$ and choose a plane $\mathbb{P}^{n-2}$ meeting $V$ transversely at $p$. Then, for each hyperplane section $H_{\lambda}\cap V$, we choose the unique irreducible component $V_{\lambda}$ containing $p$. Let $V'=\cup_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}$. They claimed that 
1.$V'$ is an open subvariety of V, and the closure of $V'$ must be V.
2.Then is follows that for generic $\lambda$, $H_{\lambda}\cap V=H_{\lambda}\cap V'$.
I could only see that $V'$ is an open subset of $V$; hence, it is an open subvariety. This is because the pencil sweeps out the whole $\mathbb{P}^{n}$. But where do the above two conclusions come from? An open subvariety can not guarantee its closure to be all of $V$. Indeed, the closure per se is not guaranteed to be a variety. I hope that anyone can give me an elementary explanation of it.

title: Should I consider the price for "option pricing" problem?
text:
I'm trying to solve the following problem from "Probability and Statistics" book by Morris H. DeGroot and Mark J. Schervish.

Suppose that common stock in the up-and-coming company A is currently priced at \$200 per share. As an incentive to get you to work for company A, you might be offered an option to buy a certain number of shares of the stock, one year from now, at a price of \$200. For simplicity, suppose that the price $X$ of the stock one year from now is a discrete random variable that can take only two values (in dollars): $260$ and $180$. Let $p$ be the probability that $X = 260$. You want to calculate the value of these stock options. (For simplicity, we shall ignore dividends and the transaction costs of buying and selling stocks.) Assume that an investor could earn 4% risk-free on any money invested for this
same year. (Assume that the 4% includes any compounding.)

I solve it in the following way. Let's say that $Y$ is an amount of money you make if you buy an option.
$$
Y = \begin{cases} 60 - c, & \mbox{with probability } p \\ -c, & \mbox{with probability } 1 - p \end{cases}
$$
where c $-$ option price. Then the amount of money you make in 1 year with this stock would be $E(Y) = p(60 - c) - c(1-p)$. On the other hand you can make $1.04c$ risk-free. Therefore a fair stock price would be:
$$
p(60 - c) - c(1-p) = 1.04c. \\
c = \frac{60p}{2.04}
$$
In the book authors for some reason ignore an option price and say that
$$
Y = \begin{cases} 60, & \mbox{with probability } p \\ 0, & \mbox{with probability } 1 - p \end{cases}
$$
I am quite puzzled as to what I miss here.

I am wondering whether there is a conceptual reason (along the lines of rank 1 groups have insufficient directions) why property (T) cannot be proven for rank $1$ like in higher rank, and how to formalize this conceptual reason. I know that this is a very imprecise question, and I would be really happy with any intuitions.

title: Optimal transport - Monge plan - measure theoretic calculation
text:
In my Optimal transport course we dealt with the Monge optimal transportation problem. We have:

a cost function $c : X \times Y \rightarrow [0, +\infty ]$.


We try to find a  probability measure $\gamma: X \times Y \rightarrow [0, 1]$  that minimizes $ \int_{X \times Y} c(x,y) d \gamma(x,y)$ where $\gamma$ satisfies $d \gamma(x,y) = d \mu(x) \delta_{T(x)}(y) dy $ for some measurable map $T: X \rightarrow Y$. Here $\delta_{x}(A) = 1$, if $x \in A$ and $\delta_{x}(A) = 0$ otherwise is the usual Dirac measure.
My problem concerns this notation: $d \gamma(x,y) = d \mu(x) \delta_{T(x)}(y) dy.$ Our professor carries out the following calculation, for example:
For a set $B \subset Y, \int_{X \times B} d \gamma(x,y) = \int_{X} ( \int_{Y} 1_{B}(y) \delta_{T(x)}(y) dy ) d\mu(x).$
This looks like an application of Fubini/ Tonelli, but the measure we integrate with respect to is not the product measure on $X \times Y.$
So, how is this calculation justified? Is this just a weird way to write integration with respect to the pushforward measure $\mu *(T)$ (defined to be for any $B \subset Y$ $\mu *(T)(B) = \mu(T^{-1}(B))$) Is this an issue with notation or am I missing something?

I am looking for a proof of this, in particular, if anyone knows the proof for my specific case of a Riemannian manifold would be better.

Standardise the vector to get a standard normal distribution.

Relate back to the original vector using the variance (trace of $(\Sigma)$ and the mean $((\mathbf{u}))$.

This approach uses the relationship between the multivariate normal distribution and the chi distribution to derive the expected value of the Euclidean norm.

title: I need Help evaluate series :$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{(x+1)(x+2)...(x+n+2)}$
text:
I need Help evaluate series :$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{(x+1)(x+2)...(x+n+2)}$$
$$s(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{(x+1)(x+2)...(x+n+2)}=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}+\frac{1}{x+1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n!}{(x+2)...(x+n+2)} $$
We have :
$$\frac{n!}{(x+2)...(x+n+2)}=\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+2)...(x+n+1)}-\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+3)...(x+n+2)}$$
Therfore:
$$s(x)=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}+\frac{1}{x+1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+2)...(x+n+1)}-\frac{1}{x+1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+3)...(x+n+2)}=\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}+s(x)-\frac{x+2}{x+1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+2)(x+3)...(x+n+2)}$$
This implies that :
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+2)(x+3)...(x+n+2)}=\frac{1}{(x+2)^2}$$
Now put x:=x-1
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(n-1)!}{(x+1)(x+2)...(x+n+1)}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{(x+1)(x+2)...(x+n+2)}=\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}$$
I faced this problem for more than an hour while trying to find a solution to it.  When I started asking the question and wrote the problem and all the details, I found the solution. title: Do we need a notion of the center of mass in special relativity?
text:
I don't see much mention of the center of mass in discussions of special relativity. I understand that there is a definition for it, but it is relatively obscure and seems to depend on mass-energy equivalence. However, I find both its obscurity and its reliance on mass-energy equivalence to be worrying, for reasons I will explain.
Starting with its obscurity. In Newtonian physics, we often like to refer to the "position" of extended bodies. We can do this naturally by referring to the location of its center of mass. This allows us to describe things like the velocity/acceleration/trajectory of extended objects. Without a clear notion of center of mass, it seems futile to even talk about "where" extended objects are located and consequently what trajectories they follow.
Next with its reliance on mass-energy. I'm referencing the answer posted at the below link, since I'm still searching for the papers the answerer linked: Is the center of mass in general relativity equal to the center of mass in newtonian gravity?
With my (admittedly still developing) understanding of relativistic dynamics, it seems that we can attribute the increase in mass of, say, a thermally excited object to the increase in difficulty it takes to change the velocities of the individual particles that make it up, due to their higher individual momenta as well as momentum's nonlinear scaling with velocity. But unless we can even understand what it means to talk about the position of an object, how can we pin down this concept rigorously? We can't talk about how difficult it is to accelerate that object, and hence it seems difficult to even talk about its mass, let alone how it relates to energy; so then how can we even say that $E=mc^2$ even applies for extended objects? I mean, we could assume energy conservation and take, say, Einstein's derivation, but it seems like we should justify that energy conservation even still works in relativity.
Apologies if my question demonstrates a bit of a misunderstanding; I suppose that is what I am trying to clear up here.

title: Entropy change of an isolated system consisting of two thermally conductive blocks of equal isochoric heat capacity at different temperatures
text:
A classic example considered in most introductory treatments of elementary thermodynamics consists of two thermally conductive (e.g., metal) blocks placed in thermal contact. In particular, I find this setup mentioned in the first half of page 56 of Enrico Fermi's classic Thermodynamics, in point 2 of page 77 of H. C. Van Ness' Understanding Thermodynamics, and in this answer (along with its comments) on Physics Stack Exchange. In all such cases, the reasoning seems to proceed as follows:
Given an isolated system consisting of two thermally conductive objects $B_1$ and $B_2$ (say, two homogeneous metal blocks of identical isochoric heat capacity $C_V$) at respective temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ with $T_1 > T_2$ which are held separately at thermal equilibrium then brought into thermal contact, we observe an amount of heat $Q$ to be transferred from $B_1$ to $B_2$. We may then express the entropy change of this isolated system as
$$\Delta S = \frac{Q_1}{T_1} + \frac{Q_2}{T_2} = \frac{-Q}{T_1} + \frac{Q}{T_2} = -\frac{Q}{T_1} + \frac{Q}{T_2} = Q\left ( \frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} \right ) = Q \left ( \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1 T_2} \right ) > 0,$$
illustrating the Second Law of Thermodynamics. This may be expressed 'differentially' as well:
Since the system is isolated and performs no work, we may use the First Law to write $ \mathrm{d} U_1 = \delta Q_1 $ and $ \mathrm{d} U_2 = -\mathrm{d} U_1 > 0$, so that
$$ \mathrm{d}S = \frac{\delta Q_1}{T_1} + \frac{\delta Q_2}{T_2} = \frac{\mathrm{d} U_1}{T_1} + \frac{\mathrm{d} U_2}{T_2} = \mathrm{d} U_1 \left (\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right )>0$$
On the other hand, couldn't we just as well analyze this process as follows:
Since the heat transfer is isobaric as well as isochoric, we have (cf. Fermi page 21),
$$ \mathrm{d} U = \frac{\partial U}{\partial T}~ \mathrm{d} T + \frac{\partial U}{\partial V}~ \mathrm{d} V = \frac{\partial U}{\partial T}~ \mathrm{d} T = C_V~ \mathrm{d} T \Longrightarrow \Delta U = C_V \Delta T,$$
so that $\Delta U_1 = C_V (T_1 - {T_{\text{avg}}})$ and $\Delta U_2 = C_V ({T_{\text{avg}}}-T_2)$ where ${T_{\text{avg}}}$ denotes the final (equilibrium) temperature attained by the system of two blocks at the conclusion of the heat exchange, given by the arithmetic mean of the two initial temperatures ${T_{\text{avg}}} = \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2}$. Then, once again using the First Law in the isochoric case $\mathrm{d} U_k = \delta Q_k = \mathrm{d} Q_k$ for $k\in\{1,2\}$ (so that $Q_k$ can be taken to be a state function by equality with the state function $U_k$), we may write
$$ \Delta S_k = \int_{T_k}^{T_{\text{avg}}} \frac{\mathrm{d} Q_k}{T}=\int_{T_k}^{T_{\text{avg}}} \frac{\mathrm{d}U_k}{T} = \int_{T_k}^{T_{\text{avg}}} \frac{C_V ~\mathrm{d}T}{T} = C_V \ln \frac{{T_{\text{avg}}}}{T_k}$$
for $k \in \{1,2\}$, so that
$$ \Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 = C_V \left ( \ln \frac{{T_{\text{avg}}}}{T_1} + \ln \frac{{T_{\text{avg}}}}{T_2} \right ) = C_V \ln \frac{{T_{\text{avg}}}^2}{T_1 T_2} $$
$$= C_V \ln \left ( \frac{T_1^2 + 2T_1 T_2 + T_2^2}{4T_1 T_2 } \right ) = C_V \ln \left ( \frac{T_1^2+ T_2^2}{4T_1 T_2 } + \frac{1}{2} \right ) .$$
Is the above analysis somehow also correct? If not, then why not? But if so, then is there some difference in perspective which has produced the apparent discrepancy between these two results for $\Delta S$?

title: Help Calculating the Electric Potential Around a Circle
text:
Consider a circle or radius $r$ and two points $P$ and $Q$ that are separated by an angular distance $\alpha$. Also, let an electric field $\vec{E}$ be constant in the $\theta$ direction: $\vec{E} = E_0 \vec{\theta}$.
Such a field can be generated from a magnetic flux $\Phi(t) = \alpha t$ crossing the circle, which would then make $E_0 = -\frac{\alpha r}{2}$
Now, if I try to calculate the potential between P to Q, I could use a line element $\rm{d}\vec{l}=r\rm{d}\theta \hat{\theta}$ and do
$$V_{P\to Q} = \int_{0}^{\alpha}(E_0r\hat{\theta})\cdot\rm{d}\theta\hat{\theta} = r E_0 \alpha$$
But if I choose going the other way around the circle, I would get
$$V_{P\to Q} = rE_02\pi -\int_{0}^{\alpha}(E_0r\hat{\theta})\cdot\rm{d}\theta\hat{\theta} = r E_0 (2\pi - \alpha)$$
But voltage is a conservative field and shouldn't depend on the path taken. What did I do wrong?

title: Why is nonzero net charge density incompatible with the cosmological principle?
text:
In an answer to a question about the overall charge-neutrality of the universe, benrg writes,

A nonzero net charge density is incompatible with the cosmological
principle. Unlike the gravitational field of a uniform mass
distribution, which can be locally gauged away, the electromagnetic
field of a uniform charge distribution has to increase linearly with
distance from a privileged center point, and the field is locally
measurable.
The reason for the homogeneous and isotropic initial conditions of the
big bang isn't known, but at least this argument shows that whatever
can produce those conditions will also produce a neutral universe.

From the similarity between the classical forms of Newton's gravitation and Coulomb's electrostatics — both of which are a coupling constant, a product of charges, and an inverse-squared distance — this distinction is not obvious.  "Gauging away" a field has always been right at the cusp of my theoretical skill, and I'm out of practice.  Can someone explain to me why these two fields behave differently?
